Victorious are the secret amorous pastimes of Rādhā and Mādhava on the banks of the Yamunā.

His mind-palace is adorned with the deeds of the goddess of speech; he is the sovereign emperor among the bards at the feet of Padmāvatī; [this work] is joined with the accounts of the amorous play of the illustrious Vāsudeva.
The poet Jayadeva composes this musical work.

Umāpatidhara causes the blossoming of speech; Jayadeva alone knows the purity of composition in words; Ācārya Govardhana is the praiseworthy refuge for those difficult to penetrate through his arrangements of the highest and truest objects of the erotic sentiment.
There was a certain renowned poet-king named Dhoyī, a master of sacred learning, with whom no rival was ever heard of.
If your mind is full of longing for the remembrance of Hari,
and if you have a curiosity for the arts of graceful play,
[then listen to] this series of sweet, soft, and beautiful words.
Then listen to the Sarasvatī of Jayadeva.
In the waters of the ocean of dissolution, you upheld the Veda,
performing the function of a ship without weariness.
O Keśava, who assumed the body of a fish; victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
The earth rests upon your exceedingly vast back,
which is made heavy by the calluses of the wheel-marks from supporting the world.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of the tortoise;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
The earth rests upon the tip of your tusk,
submerged as if it were a digit of the spot upon the moon.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
Upon your excellent lotus-hand, the nail is a wondrous horn that has crushed the bee-like body of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of the Man-lion;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
O Wondrous Dwarf, you who subdued Bali through your stride; O Purifier of people, born from the water of your toenails!
O Keśava, who assumed the form of Vāmana;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
In the world consisting of the blood of Kṣatriyas, you bathe [the earth], which is free from sin and has its torments of existence pacified, in water.
O Keśava, who assumed the form of the Lord of the Bhṛgus;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
In battle, you scatter in all directions the desirable tribute from the crowns of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s heads— a tribute once coveted by the lords of the quarters.
O Keśava, who assumed the body of Rāma;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
Upon your fair body you wear a garment with the luster of a cloud,
resembling the Yamunā as she meets [the Ganges] out of fear of the blow of the plow.
O Keśava, who have assumed the form of the wielder of the plow;
victory to you, O Lord of the world, Hare!
Alas! O Compassionate One, you censure the Vedic tradition that ordains sacrifice and prescribes the slaughter of animals.
O Keśava, who assumed the body of Buddha! Victory to you, O Lord of the World, Hare!
In the destruction of the multitudes of barbarians,
you wield your sword like a terrifying comet of some indescribable kind.
O Keśava, who has assumed the body of Kalki;
victory to You, O Lord of the World, Hare!
Listen to this noble utterance of the poet Śrī Jayadeva; it bestows happiness, grants auspiciousness, and is the very essence of existence.
O Keśava, who has assumed the tenfold form;
victory to you, O Lord of the World, Hare!
He who rescued the Vedas, sustained the world, supported the earth, shattered the Daitya, deceived Bali, brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas,
conquered Rāvaṇa, wielded the plow, and extended compassion.
Salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, who, having assumed ten forms, causes the Mlecchas to swoon.
O Lord of Jayadeva, O Hari! You who rest upon the orb of Lakṣmī’s breasts, you who wear earrings, and you who bear the charming forest garland—victory, victory to you!
O ornament of the circle of sun-gems, O destroyer of worldly existence,
O swan in the minds of the sages, victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O vanquisher of the serpent Kaliya who bears deadly poison, O delighter of the people, O sun to the lotus of the Yadu clan—victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari! JAYADEVA! HARE!
O destroyer of Madhu, Mura, and Naraka; O you who have Garuḍa as your seat; O source of sport for the host of gods; victory, victory to you, O Lord Hari!
O Lord whose eyes are like the petals of a stainless lotus, O deliverer from worldly existence!
O Hari, the source and treasure of the three worlds, victory, victory to you, O God!
O Hare, Lord of Victory, who adorned the daughter of Janaka, who conquered Dūṣaṇa, and who subdued the Ten-necked Rāvaṇa in battle— be victorious, be victorious!

O Lord Hari, Jayadeva, conquer, conquer! You who are as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, who held Mount Mandara [at the churning of the ocean], and who are the cakora bird for the moon of Your glorious face.
This auspicious and radiant song by the poet Śrī Jayadeva brings joy; victory, victory to you, O Lord Jayadeva, O Hari!

The chest of Madhusūdana is sealed with saffron from its embrace against the slopes of Padmā’s breasts; it appears as if manifesting passion, with the flood of perspiration from the exhaustion of sporting Love clearly visible.
May he fulfill your dear wish.
In the spring, with limbs as delicate as the blossoms of the *vāsantī* flower,
she wanders through the forest, having repeatedly followed Kṛṣṇa;
she is intensely distressed by the anxiety born of the fever of love.
Her companion, whose distress was evident, spoke these words full of pathos to Rādhā.
In the Malaya breeze, tender from its caressing of the *lalita-lavaṅga* creeper;
in the bower-cottages of the groves, where the warbling of cuckoos is intermingled with swarms of bees.
O friend, Hari dwells here in this spring season full of emotion; he dances together with young women, which is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.
In the lamentation produced by the wives of travelers whose desires are maddened by love,
amidst the clusters of bakula trees crowded with swarms of bees and filled with masses of blossoms;
O friend, Hari dwells here in this springtime full of emotion; he dances together with young women, which is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.
In that grove where the *tamāla* trees, with their fresh leaves, were submissive to the intensity of the musk-fragrance,
and where the clusters of *kiṃśuka* flowers shone like the luster of the nails of the Mind-born God as he tore open the hearts of young men;
Hari dwells here in the springtime of the lake,
O friend, and dances together with young women— a sight that is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.
When the filaments and flowers of the *pāṭalī* trees have blossomed, possessing the luster of the golden staffs of King Madana,
and when they display the grace of Cupid’s quiver through the swarms of bees that have gathered upon them;
Hari dwells here in the springtime full of emotion;
O friend, he dances together with young women—this is unbearable for one separated from their beloved.
O you who have brought forth a youthful smile at the sight of the world overcome with shame;
O you whose jagged ketaka flowers, shaped like the points of spears that mow down those separated from their lovers, fill the quarters of the sky!
Hari dwells here in this spring season full of emotion; O friend, he dances together with young women, which is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.
Delightful with the fragrance of *mādhavikā* flowers, sweetly scented with *navamālikā* and *jāti*,
enchanting even the minds of sages, and a causeless friend to the young.
O friend, Hari dwells here in this flowery springtime; he dances together with young women—a sight that is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.

In the forest grove of Vṛndāvana, purified by the waters of the Yamunā flowing along its borders, where the mango trees have blossomed and bristled with thrill at the embrace of the trembling atimukta vines.
O friend, Hari dwells here in this flowery springtime; he dances together with young women, which is unbearable for those separated from their lovers.

This description of the forest in the season of the passionate spring, composed by Śrī Jayadeva, which has the essence of the remembrance of Hari’s feet and follows the transformations of love, now arises.
Hari dwells here in this springtime full of emotion; O friend, he dances together with the young women—a sight that is unbearable for one separated from their beloved.
Here, indeed, the kinsman of the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower burns the heart— perfuming the forests with the manifest scents of cloth-like pollen from *mallī* creepers shattered by the wind.
The wind, possessing a power like that of his spreading, incomparable arrows, blew forth.

How, indeed, are travelers made to pass [the time] by means of moments of focused meditation, while their ears are set ablaze with the feverish cries of playful cuckoos and the rustling of mango sprouts shaken by bees greedy for the scent of blooming honey?
These days pass in the exuberance of the aesthetic delight arising from the union with the vital breath and the mind.

Pointing out from afar Murāri, who was intensely longing for the charming and playful gestures flashing with the excitement of embracing many women, that female companion spoke again to Rādhikā in her presence.
His dark body is anointed with sandalwood paste; he wears yellow garments and a forest garland;
his pair of cheeks is adorned with jeweled earrings that sway in play; and he is radiant with a smile.
O playful woman, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young wives who are intent on amorous play.
Embracing Hari with passion by the weight of her full breasts,
a certain cowherd maiden sang along, raising the *pañcama* note.
O playful woman, here Hari sports among this multitude of charming young wives who are intent on amorous play.
A certain charming young woman meditates intensely upon the lotus-face of the Slayer of Madhu, which excites the mind with the playful movement of her eyes, flickering with amorous grace.
O playful one, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young women who are intent on amorous play.
A certain woman with beautiful hips pressed her cheek against his and whispered something at the root of his ear; she kissed her beloved tenderly as he was filled with thrills of joy.
O playful one, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young women who are intent on amorous play.
And out of curiosity for the arts of play, a certain woman drew him by the hem of his silk garment with her hand as he had gone to a lovely grove of *vañjula* trees on the bank of the Yamunā.
O playful woman, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young wives who are intent on amorous play.

In the delight of the *rāsa* dance, a young woman, intent on dancing together with Hari to the sweet sounds produced by the rows of bracelets trembling against her palms as she clapped her hands, was praised.
O playful one, Hari sports here amidst this multitude of charming young women who are intent on amorous play.
He embraces one woman, kisses another, delights yet another beautiful lady, gazes with a smile at a different one, and follows after a charming woman.
O playful one, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young women who are intent on amorous play.
May this *lalita* (charming) secret of the wonderful pastimes of Keśava by the poet Śrī Jayadeva, performed in the forest of Vṛndāvana, spread auspiciousness and glory.
O playful woman, Hari sports here among this multitude of charming young wives who are intent on amorous play.
Creating joy for all through his enchanting grace, bringing about a festival of love with limbs as dark and tender as a row of blue lotuses,
he was embraced at will on every limb by the beautiful women of Vraja from all sides.
O friend, in this springtime, Hari, charming as if the personification of the erotic sentiment itself, is at play.
Today, as if from the distress of being swallowed by the serpent dwelling upon his lap,

the breeze from the Sandalwood Mountain pursues the Lord’s mountain with a desire to plunge into the frost; moreover, having beheld the buds at the tops of the succulent mango trees, it rises out of joy.
The sweet and soaring songs of the cuckoos break forth here and there with the cry of "kuhū, kuhū."
Rādhā dwelt in the forest with Hari, whose love was shared by all;
yet, due to her own pride having dissolved, she went elsewhere out of the power of jealousy.
At one point, in a bower of creepers filled with swarms of humming bees—
Perched on the peak of the Mukhara mountain, though distressed, she spoke in secret to her friend.
His enchanting flute resounds with the sweet sound of the nectar flowing from his moving lower lip;
his earrings sway against his cheeks as his head moves with the flickering corners of his eyes.
My mind remembers Hari here in the *rāsa* dance, who performed his amorous play and directed his jests toward me.
His hair is encircled by a halo like the beautiful crest of a peacock with its eye-patterns;
his fine appearance is enhanced by thick clouds colored by the abundant rainbows of Indra.
My mind remembers Hari here in the *rāsa* dance, who performed his amorous play and directed his jests toward me.
[The face] which has acquired the desire to kiss the mouth of the cowherd girl whose hips are like a cluster of *gopaka* flowers,
and which possesses the beauty of a radiant smile upon its sweet lower lip like a *bandhujīva* bud.
My mind remembers Hari here in the *rāsa* dance, who performed his amorous play and offered me a jest.
Surrounded by thousands of young cowherd women whose sprout-like arms were covered in profuse horripilation,
the darkness was dispelled by the rays from the clusters of jewel ornaments upon their hands, feet, and chests.
My mind remembers Hari here in the *rāsa* dance, who displayed his playful charms and offered me jests.
Her forehead is adorned with a sandalwood tilaka that mocks the moon as it emerges from a mass of clouds;
her heart, like a door-panel, is merciless in its crushing of the circles of her full, firm breasts.
My mind remembers Hari here in the rāsa dance, who performed his amorous sports and offered playful jests.
His cheeks are adorned with magnificent earrings made of charming makaras fashioned from jewels;
he wears yellow garments and is surrounded by a noble retinue of sages, humans, gods, and asuras.
My mind remembers Hari here in the rāsa dance, who performed his amorous play and directed playful jests toward me.
At the foot of a lush kadamba tree, he stands meeting [his beloved], quelling the fear of the defilement of this Kali age;
may he also delight my mind with some indescribable glance that stirs the god of love.
My mind remembers Hari here at the rāsa dance, who performed his amorous play and directed playful jests toward me.
This exceedingly beautiful and enchanting form of the enemy of Madhu, described by Śrī Jayadeva,
is now worthy of those possessed of merit who remember the feet of Hari.
My mind remembers Hari here in the rāsa dance, who performed his amorous play and directed his jests toward me.
He counts the multitude of virtues [of others], yet he does not seek even out of delusion to perceive a fault; he carries great contentment and casts away defects far away—
O Kṛṣṇa, who sports with young women whose thirst for him turns toward you, and who exists even without me!
Furthermore, my mind again creates a contrary desire; what shall I do?
Having gone at night into the secret bower-house, she beheld him dwelling there in solitude,
his entire gaze darting about with alarm, yet laughing with the intensity of the passion of love.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a state of passionate agitation.
At their first meeting, she, abashed, became compliant through hundreds of clever endearments;
with her soft and sweet smiles and speech, she loosened the silk garment from her hips.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love and full of passion.
Having rested for a long time upon my very chest, reclining on a bed of young shoots,
she embraced me and drank from my lower lip after I had likewise embraced and kissed her.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a state of passionate agitation.
With eyes half-closed in languor, her cheeks graced by a line of horripilation,
and her entire body drenched in the perspiration of exertion, she was exceedingly restless from the intoxication of supreme passion.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love and manifesting my passion.
She surpassed the deliberations of the science of love with the sweet warbling of the cuckoo’s cry;
her tresses were disheveled with loose flowers, and she bore the weight of her firm breasts marked by nail-scratches.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a state of passionate emotion.
With the canopy of love-making filled by the tinkling of jeweled anklets on her feet,
and with the jingling of her loosened girdle, she gave him kisses while grasping his hair.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love and manifesting my passion.
With her lotus-like eyes slightly closed in languor from the essence of the occasion of amorous pleasure,
her slender vine-like body falling listlessly, she [beheld] Madhusūdana, who had awakened the god of love.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a manner full of passion.
May this work, composed by Śrī Jayadeva, which possesses the nature of the exceedingly sweet amorous dalliance of the Enemy of Mura,
and which describes the longing of the cowherd women, spread joy with its graceful charm.
O friend, delight the noble slayer of Keśin with me, who am filled with the longing of love, in a manner full of passion.

In the forest, having looked up at me— who was embarrassed, whose flute had slipped from my hand, whose creeper-like eyebrows were arched, who was being watched by the corners of the eyes of the cowherd girls moving toward me, whose cheeks were moist with excessive perspiration, and whose face was charming with the nectar of a smile— [He departed].
I see Govinda, surrounded by the multitude of the beautiful women of Vraja, and I rejoice.
The blossoming of the young *aśoka* creeper, with its clusters of buds difficult to behold,
and even the breeze from the groves by the lake causes pain;
for though made charming by the humming of wandering bees, the bud does not open.
O friend, this *śikhariṇī* mango tree delights me with its blossoming fruit.
Even the enemy of Kaṃsa, having placed Rādhā in his heart, abandoned the beautiful women of Vraja— the very chains that bind one to the latent impressions of saṃsāra.
Having searched for Rādhikā here and there, his mind distressed by the wounds of Cupid’s arrows,
Mādhava felt remorse and despaired within a bower on the banks of the Yamunā.
Seeing me surrounded by a multitude of brides, she moved away;
out of a sense of guilt, she did not restrain me either, being overcome by extreme fear.
O Hari-Hari, she has gone away as if angry, due to her lack of respect.
What will she do, what will she say after this long separation? What use have I for wealth, for people, for life, or for my home?
Having lost her respect for Hari and Hari, she departed as if in anger.
I contemplate her face with its arched brows and weight of anger,
like a red lotus above which a restless bee is hovering.
O Hari, Hari! Having lost all regard for me, she has departed as if in anger.
I constantly and intensely delight her who dwells within my heart; why do I wander in the forest for her sake, and why do I lament here in vain?
Having lost her respect for Hari and Hari, she departed as if in anger.
O slender one, I perceive that your heart is distressed by resentment;
therefore, I do not know where you have gone, nor do I offer you any conciliation.
She has gone away as if angry, out of disregard for Hari and Hara.
You appear before me and cause me only to come and go;
why do you not give me an embrace with such urgency as in the past?
Having lost her respect for Hari and Hari, she departed as if in anger.
"Forgive me; never again shall I act in such a manner.
O beautiful one, grant me your sight, for I am tormented by the god of love."
O Hari, Hari! Having lost her respect, she has departed as if in anger.
This [work] concerning Hari has been described by Jayadeva,
who is devoted to Him and who is the beloved of Rohiṇī, born from the ocean of the Kindubilva lineage.
O Hari, O Hari! Having lost her respect, she has departed as if in anger.

This necklace upon my heart is a lotus-stalk strand, not a lord of serpents; this row of blue-lotus petals around my neck is not the luster of poison; this sandalwood powder is not ashes—O you who delight in embracing me!
O Anaṅga, strike him; why do you run in anger, mistaking him for Hara?
Do not place this mango-arrow in your hand, nor string your bow;
O conqueror of the universe through play, what is the point of this manly prowess that strikes people into a swoon?
[It is no match for] the arrows of the flickering side-glances of that very fawn-eyed woman, which are loosed by the Mind-born God.
Even now, my mind, though slightly worn by the stages of spiritual progress, does not yet kindle [into full realization].
Let the arrow of her sidelong glance, fixed upon the bow of her brow, pierce my vital organs;
let her dark, curling mass of hair, like the embodiment of Māra, stir up my passion; and let this bimba-fruit lip, glowing with redness, O slender one, spread delusion throughout me.
How can he, whose circle of breasts possesses such virtuous conduct, play with my life-breaths?
Those pleasures of touch, those tremulous and affectionate glances of her eyes, that fragrance of her lotus-face, that curvature of her speech which flows like nectar,
and that sweetness of her bimba-like lips— if, even amidst attachment to such objects, the mind [remains undisturbed]...
Alas, how can the disease of separation increase for her while she is fixed in meditative absorption?

In her, who was a moving deity for the conquest of the bodiless god of love, Smara made her creeper-like eyebrows his bow, the undulating waves of her sidelong glances his arrows, and the curve of her ear-lobe his string.
Why have weapons that have conquered the worlds been offered?
In a bower of cane thickets on the bank of the Yamunā,
Rādhikā’s friend spoke to Mādhava, who was resting gently and agitated by the weight of his love.
She censures sandalwood and finds distress from the rays of the moon;
she regards the breeze from the Malaya mountains as if it were poison, because it meets with the abode of serpents.
O Mādhava, in separation from you, that wretched woman has, as it were, merged into you through meditation out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
As if from the incessant falling of the arrows of Love, he makes a shield for the protection of his own heart against you— a broad lattice of water-laden lotus petals— over its vital core.
O Mādhava, in your absence, that wretched woman has, as it were, merged into you through meditation out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
This bed of flowers, lovely with its many arts of grace and serving as a couch for the arrows of the flower-arrowed god,
prepares a floral bed for you, like a religious vow, for the sake of the pleasure of your embrace.
O Mādhava, in your absence, that wretched woman has become absorbed in you through meditation, as if out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
And his noble lotus-face bears a weight of flowing tears,
like the moon with a stream of nectar trickling from its being crushed by the fangs of a monstrous Rāhu.
O Mādhava, in separation from you, that wretched woman has, as it were, merged into you through meditation out of fear of the arrows of the mind-born god.
In secret, she draws you—who have become the peerless god of love—with musk from the deer;
she bows to the sea-monster while placing beneath it an arrow made of fresh mango blossoms in her hand.
O Mādhava, in separation from you, that wretched woman has, as it were, merged into you through meditation out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
Mādhava, at every step she says this as well: "I have fallen at your feet;
when you turn away from me, even the ocean of nectar instantly spreads a burning heat throughout my body."
O Mādhava, in separation from you, that wretched woman has merged into you through meditation, as if out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
Having first visualized you as being exceedingly difficult to attain due to the torpor of meditation,
she laments, laughs, desponds, weeps, trembles, and releases her fever of passion.
O Mādhava, in separation from you, that wretched woman has, as it were, merged into you through meditation out of fear of the arrows of the god of love.
If this, composed by the illustrious Jayadeva, is deemed worthy by your mind, then it should be danced;
the speech of the friend of the young cowherd girl, distressed by separation from Hari, should be recited.
O Mādhava, in your absence, that wretched woman has merged into you through meditation, as if out of fear of the arrows of the mind-born god of love.
Her dwelling acts like a forest; even the garland of her dear friend acts like a snare;
even the heat of her sighing acts like a mass of flames from a forest fire;
alas, in separation from you, she too—poor thing—takes on the form of a doe. Oh, how can this be?
Even Kandarpa acts like Yama when he performs the Śārdūlavikrīḍita dance.

she of the slender form considered it an excessive burden.

carries a constant burning as if it were the fire of passion itself.
O Keśava, [this is] during your separation from Rādhikā.

She bristles with horripilation, hisses, laments, trembles, faints,
meditates, wanders in delusion, wilts, falls down, rises up, and even swoons.
O slender-limbed one, would she not live out of passion for you in such a state of intense fever?
O you who resemble the physician of heaven, if you are pleased, the Ender (Death) will not prevail over one who has been abandoned [by you]. Otherwise, he will not.

O Physician of the Gods, dear to the heart, you do not free Rādhā from her affliction—she who is tormented by love and can be cured only by the nectar of contact with your limbs; therefore, O Upendra, you are more cruel even than the thunderbolt.
It is a marvel that for a long time the mind of this woman— whose body is afflicted by the fever of the god of love—
has been tormented by thoughts of sandalwood, the moon, and lotus ponds;
yet, under the power of exhaustion, she longs only for you, her beloved, whose very form is cool.
Meditating while staying in solitude, she somehow breathes for a moment, though utterly exhausted.
How can she, who formerly could not endure separation from you for even a moment— she who was exhausted by the mere closing of her eyes—
now breathe near the branch of a mango tree?
Having gazed upon the flowering tips after a long separation...
"I dwell here; go, entreat Rādhā in my name, and bring her back.
Thus commissioned by the Enemy of Mura, the friend herself approached and spoke this again to Rādhā.
When the Malaya breeze blows, bringing with it the god of love,
the clusters of blossoms burst open to shatter the hearts of those separated from their lovers.
O friend, in separation from you, the wearer of the forest garland languishes.
When the moon of cool rays burns him, he mimics death;
when the arrow of Love falls upon him, he laments, utterly distraught.
O friend, in separation from you, the wearer of the forest garland languishes.
When the swarm of bees hums, she covers her ears;
in her heart, filled with the pang of separation, she suffers pain night after night.
O friend, in separation from you, the one wearing a forest garland is perishing.
He dwells under the canopy of the forest, abandons his graceful abode,
rolls upon the bed of the earth, and repeatedly utters your name.
O friend, in separation from you, the wearer of the forest garland is perishing.
The poet Jayadeva says: by means of the amorous pastimes of one separated from her beloved, may Hari arise in the mind through the power of merit when it is filled with impetuous emotion.

O charming Rādhikā, follow Madhumathana who has gone before you.

Listen to the most delightful warbling of the cuckoos, which charms young women like bees; cultivate a deep devotion toward these flocks of birds that proclaim the command of the one whose bow is made of flowers.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the Slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.
O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, this cluster of creepers, with its mass of young shoots trembling in the wind, seems to urge you forward; therefore, abandon your lingering pace.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the Slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.

Ask this jar-like breast, which throbs as if under the influence of the waves of passion and reveals the embrace of Hari, and which possesses a stream of pure water in the form of its charming necklace.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.
O fierce one, this body of yours has been perceived in its entirety by all your friends as ready for the battle of love;
come now, shamelessly and with passion, to the sound of your tinkling girdle acting as a drum.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the Slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.
Supporting her friend with a hand whose nails are as charming as the arrows of Love, she playfully awakens even Hari— who is himself habituated to her gait— with the tinkling of her moving bracelets.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the Slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.
May that which was spoken by Śrī Jayadeva— surpassing necklaces and setting aside all else—
dwell eternally upon the throat of those whose minds are fixed on Hari.
O charming Rādhikā, follow the slayer of Madhu who has gone before you.
"She will see me; she will speak with me of love through embraces limb by limb;
she will attain joy and delight upon meeting her friend"—distraught with such thoughts, he gazes at you, trembles, his hair stands on end, he rejoices, and he perspires.
The beloved comes forth and faints within the bower, a dense mass of profound darkness.

O friend, in the bower, the hearts of those rogues eager for their secret trysts are everywhere— [hearts] upon whose eyes they cast collyrium, upon whose ears a cluster of *tāpiccha* blossoms, upon whose head a wreath of dark lotuses, and upon whose breasts the musk-leaf design.
The darkness, as lovely as a blue garment, embraces every limb of the fair-eyed women.

This darkness, as black as the leaf of the *tamāla* tree, is streaked on all sides with lines of light from the clusters of radiance belonging to those women going to meet their lovers, whose bodies are fair like those of Kashmir.
It acts as a touchstone for the gold of love for Him.

Having beheld Hari at the entrance of his bower-abode, which was illuminated by the luster of the gems in his necklaces, strings of pearls, shimmering waist-bands, armlets, bracelets, and jeweled ornaments;
Then a female friend spoke to the bashful Rādhā.
O you whose face is radiant with the laughter of passionate love-play, sport in this most charming bower, the very abode of dalliance!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
Sport, O you whose jar-like breasts have trembling necklaces, upon the essence of a bed made of fresh *aśoka* leaves!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
O you whose body is as delicate as a flower, sport in this dwelling-place of pure garments fashioned from heaps of blossoms!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
O you who are cool and fragrant with the breeze from the moving Malaya forests; O you who shine forth with charming songs overflowing with aesthetic flavor!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
In this state, which is as full of the essence of passion as it is resonant with the humming of swarms of bees delighted by honey, sport!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
Sport in this place made resonant by the exceedingly sweet warbling of flocks of cuckoos,
where the peaks are radiant with the luster of your gleaming teeth.
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
O you with heavy, full hips and languid grace, sport for a long time in this place thick with the new sprouts of spreading vine-like arms.
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
O Murāri, bestow hundreds of blessings upon the assembly of Padmāvatī’s happiness,
as the royal poet Jayadeva proclaims!
Enter here, O Rādhā, into the presence of Mādhava.
Carrying you in his heart for a long time, he is utterly exhausted and deeply tormented by Kandarpa; he now desires to drink from your lower lip, which is like a bimba fruit overflowing with nectar.
Adorn this body of his here for a moment with even a fraction of the beauty of a playful arching of your brow.
When one has served the lotus-feet [of the Buddha] like a purchased slave, how could there be any agitation?
With eyes restless upon Govinda, filled with both agitation and joy,
she entered her dwelling while her charming anklets tinkled.
His face was marked by various shifting expressions blossoming at the sight of Rādhā’s countenance,
like the ocean whose lofty waves are stirred by the sight of the moon’s orb.

She beheld Hari, whose singular essence is eternal bliss, whose playful charms she had long desired, who was the abode of the god of love, and whose face was rendered submissive by the power of intense joy.
Embracing him from afar as he wears a necklace of exceedingly pure pearls upon his chest,
she was like the flood of the Yamunā’s waters mingled with a mass of clearly visible foam.
She beheld Hari, whose aesthetic flavor is singular, whose playful charms she had long desired,
whose face was submissive under the power of great joy, and who is the dwelling place of the god of love.
His dark and tender body is adorned with a white silk garment,
like a blue lotus whose root is encircled by a dense mass of yellow pollen.
She beheld Hari, whose singular essence is eternal, whose playful charms she had long desired, the abode of the god of love, his countenance overcome by the weight of profound joy.
Her face, enchanting with the movement of the corners of her tremulous eyes, generates a passion of delight,
like an autumnal pond where a pair of wagtails sport within the heart of a blooming lotus.
She beheld Hari, whose singular essence is eternal, whose playful charms she had long desired, the abode of the god of love, his face rendered submissive by the power of profound joy.
It possesses the beauty of earrings like the sun meeting with the lotus of his face;
it arouses longing for delight through the sprout-like lower lip, which shines brilliantly with the luster of a smile.
She beheld Hari, whose singular essence is eternal play as desired,
his face submissive under the power of great joy, the very abode of the god of love.
With its interior as beautiful as a cloud streaked by moonbeams and filled with flower-buds,
it bears the application of a sandalwood tilaka as pure as the orb of the moon risen from the darkness.
She beheld Hari, whose singular essence is eternal, whose playful pastimes were long desired,
whose face was submissive under the power of great joy, and who is the dwelling place of the bodiless god of love.
His body was made uneven by a heavy burden of horripilation through the arts of amorous play;
it was restless, and his form was made beautiful by ornaments radiant with the mass of rays from clusters of jewels.
She beheld Hari, whose aesthetic flavor is singular, whose playful charms she had long desired, who dwells within the heart of the bodiless god of love, and whose face was overcome with profound joy.

Having placed for a long time within your hearts Hari— the essence of the fruits of meritorious deeds, whose majesty is extolled by Śrī Jayadeva and whose burden of ornaments is doubled [in splendor]— bow down to him.

She beheld Hari, whose essence is singular, who for long has been the object of her desired pastimes, whose face is submissive under the power of intense joy, and who is the abode of the bodiless god of love.

Now, at the moment of beholding her beloved, Rādhā’s eyes— whose pupils were exceedingly tremulous as if from the exertion of traveling beyond the corners of the eyes to reach the very limits of the ears— fell [upon him].
A flood of tears of joy fell like a spreading stream of perspiration.
As she leaned toward the edge of the bed, her smile concealed by a feigned scratch, and as the circle of her confidantes and attendants had departed from the house,
she gazed upon the face of her beloved, which was made auspicious by the intent glances of the arrows of Love.
Even the modesty of that fawn-eyed woman, though possessed of shame, seemed to depart far away.
When the circle of her friends had departed, he beheld Rādhā— her lower lip bathed in a broad smile that overflowed with intentions overcome by passion and laden with no small weight of bashfulness—
and seeing her heart full of longing, [he approached] her repeatedly with fresh sprouts.
Hari spoke to his beloved, whose eyes were fixed upon the bed where their child had been placed.
O lovely one, place your lotus-feet upon the bed of tender sprouts; let this well-adorned bed experience the defeat of its enemy, your blossoming feet.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
With my lotus-like hand, I touch your feet; you have come from afar.
Grant me a moment’s favor upon your bed, like an anklet that follows its brave master.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
Compose words that are agreeable, like nectar flowing from the treasury of the nectar of your face;
I shall remove the silken garment from my breast that obstructs my bosom, as if removing the pain of separation.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
Place the jar of your breasts upon my chest— trembling with the thrill of the sudden embrace of your beloved and difficult to attain— and thus extinguish the fever of the mind-born god.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
O beautiful lady, bring the nectar of your lower lip and revive this servant as if he were dead—
he whose mind is fixed upon you, whose body is consumed by the fire of separation, and who is devoid of all grace.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
O moon-faced one, cause your jeweled girdle-string to tinkle with a sound that harmonizes with the resonance of your throat;
with it, soothe the long-standing distress in my pair of ears, which have been deprived of the cuckoo’s song.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
Cease now and abandon this exhaustion of passion; do not look upon me, who am now rendered distraught by your utterly fruitless anger, with this eye of yours that seems as if closed in shame.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
May this work, composed by Śrī Jayadeva, which proclaims at every step the joy of the Enemy of Madhu,
produce for those who possess aesthetic sensitivity a delightful diversion consisting of the very nature of passionate love.
O Rādhikā, for a moment now follow Nārāyaṇa as he departs.
In the midst of the tumultuous onset of battle for the sake of amorous play upon Māra’s lap, she began with a certain boldness to conquer her lover; yet,
out of agitation, her hip-region became motionless, her vine-like arms grew limp, and her body trembled.
With chest heaving and eyes closed, how could the heroic sentiment ever be realized in women?
Then Rādhā, who had her husband under her control and was free from all obstacles, though weary from lovemaking, spoke to her beloved out of a desire for adornment.
O delight of the Yadus, place here upon your breast— a breast that is as cool as sandalwood and a twin to the auspicious jars of the God of Love— a decorative leaf-pattern made of musk.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he played, bringing delight to her heart.

O beloved, brighten your eyes—those collyrium-appliances that put to shame the swarms of bees, which serve as the arrows discharged by the God of Love; eyes upon which kohl has settled from kissing your lower lip.
She spoke thus while the delighter of the Yadus was sporting with her, bringing joy to her heart.

O you of auspicious appearance, place these earrings upon the circle of your ears, which cause the expansion and contraction of the deer-like pupils of the eyes, and which bear the playful charm of the noose of the Mind-born God.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he was sporting, bringing delight to her heart.
Arrange for a long time before me, upon my face, a beautiful mass of hair like a swarm of bees—
hair that surpasses the lotus, is stainless, well-groomed, and brings forth laughter.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he was sporting, bringing delight to her heart.
O lotus-faced one, whose brow-moon has its fatigue-drops stilled, place this graceful tilaka-mark, smeared with the essence of musk, which bears a touch of the dark spot.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he played, bringing delight to her heart.
O giver of honor, fashion my lovely tresses into chowries for the banner of the Mind-born God;
let them be beautiful with flowers fallen from Rati’s embrace and as dazzling as the crests of peacocks.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he was sporting, bringing delight to her heart.

O you of pure intent, O beautiful one, clothe your charming and firm hips— which are like the caves of Śambara’s elephant-slayer and are thick with flesh— with garments, jeweled girdles, and ornaments.
She spoke thus while the delighter of the Yadus was sporting, bringing joy to her heart.
O Maṇḍana, make your heart tender toward the charming words of Śrī Jayadeva,
which shatter the fever of worldly existence and the impurities of the Kali age through the nectar of remembering Hari’s feet.
She spoke thus to the joy of the Yadus as he was sporting, bringing delight to her heart.
Fashion a leaf-design upon your breasts; paint colorful patterns on your cheeks; fasten your girdle upon your hips; arrange your heavy braid with a garland;
place a row of bracelets upon your hand, and set anklets upon your feet.
Thus addressed, the one clad in yellow garments was pleased and acted accordingly.
Whatever skill in the arts of music, whatever meditation upon Viṣṇu, whatever essence of the discernment of the erotic sentiment, and whatever playful artistry in poetry—
all that belongs to the learned poet Jayadeva, whose soul is entirely absorbed in Kṛṣṇa alone.
May the wise, filled with joy, purify [this work] from the Śrīgītagovinda.

May this poem, the *Śrīgītagovinda*, composed by Śrī Jayadeva— the son of Rāmādevī and born of the illustrious Bhojadeva— reside upon the throats of the beloved circle of sages beginning with Parāśara.
